newsitem.title: USA: BPA does not expect to be power buyer this winter.
newsitem.headline: BPA does not expect to be power buyer this winter.

text.p: The Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), though currently taking delivery of power it swapped this summer with Southwest utilities, said it does not expect to be a big buyer of power this winter.
Citing contingency studies, "it doesn't look like we will need to purchase--maybe for off-peak," said a power operations specialist at Portland, Ore.-based Bonneville.

He noted BPA, a federal agency marketing power from the Columbia River dams, has the option of drawing on water in western Canadian reservoirs and would "prefer to do that rather than purchase energy."
Although the water year, which runs from October through September, has just started, it so far appears to be near normal conditions, industry sources have said.
"Last year was an anomaly," the Bonneville source said, referring to 1995-96's remarkably high precipitation levels.
"This year looks closer to a normal year."
Hydroelectric output last winter was so high BPA turned back some of the power delivered to it under long-term swap agreeements.

Precipitation in parts of the Northwest was unusually high in October, but most of it fell on the west side of the Cascade mountains, at lower elevations where any early snowpack probably will melt before winter sets in for good.
Currently, southbound power transmissions on the Pacific Intertie, the major high voltage lines linking the Northwest and Southwest, continue to outpace volumes headed north.
During early morning hours, however, net transmissions are northbound, largely due to swap paybacks for energy BPA delivered to the Southwest during the summer, the agency said.
For other hours, southbound volumes slightly outweigh tranmissions from the Northwest.
"During a general average year, at some point you would see net imports into the Northwest," the Bonneville source said. "But we won't hit critical loads until December or January."
Bonneville has been in and out of the surplus power market during October, raising prices by $4.00 to $5.00 per megawatt hour over the course of the month.
Water supplies in the Northwest are said to be tight right now due to seasonal declines as streambeds dry up, rationing relaterd to fish spawning and end-of-year reservoir targets.
"Right now we are filling and getting ready for winter peaking demand," said the BPA power operations specialist.
"Last year at this time everything was full."
